biomaterials-001.question: Which statement correctly describes the idea of biocompatibility for biomaterials?
choices: Only materials that do not react with the body at all inside it are biocompatible
The ability to perform the required function in a specific application with an appropriate host response
A material that contains no toxic elements can be said to be biocompatible in any application
biomaterials-001.explanation: Biocompatibility is not an intrinsic property of a material; it is defined as "the ability of a material to perform with an appropriate host response in a specific application". Alumina and zirconia, which do not react with bone, suit the femoral heads of artificial hip joints, but materials that fill bone defects are actually expected to react, by bonding to bone or by being resorbed and replaced by bone. Because the desirable response differs by application in this way, not reacting at all is not a requirement. And even a material with no toxic elements is not compatible with an application if it is so stiff that it causes stress shielding, if its wear debris causes inflammation, or if it forms thrombi in contact with blood. The shape, surface condition and location of use are evaluated as well.

biomaterials-002.question: Which of these is a bioactive ceramic that bonds directly and chemically to bone?
choices: Hydroxyapatite
High-purity alumina
Yttria partially stabilized zirconia
biomaterials-002.explanation: Hydroxyapatite (Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂) is a calcium phosphate with nearly the same composition as the mineral component of bones and teeth; in the body a layer of the same kind of apatite as bone forms on its surface, and it bonds directly to bone. Because of this property it is used as a filler for bone defects and as a surface coating on metal implants. Bioactive glass bonds to bone in the same way. High-purity alumina and partially stabilized zirconia are bioinert ceramics that hardly react in the body; being hard and wear resistant, they are used for the femoral heads of artificial hip joints, but they do not bond chemically to bone. Their surfaces are either covered by a thin fibrous membrane or only interlock mechanically with bone.

biomaterials-003.question: What is the Ca/P molar ratio of hydroxyapatite, Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂?
biomaterials-003.explanation: The formula contains 10 Ca and 6 P (from the 6 PO₄ groups), so Ca/P = 10/6 ≈ 1.67. Bone apatite contains carbonate ions and other species, and its Ca/P is somewhat lower than this. 1.50 is the ratio 3/2 of tricalcium phosphate (TCP, Ca₃(PO₄)₂). β-TCP is more soluble than hydroxyapatite and is used as a bioresorbable material that is resorbed in the body and replaced by bone. 1.33 is the ratio 8/6 of octacalcium phosphate (Ca₈H₂(PO₄)₆·5H₂O). If the Ca/P ratio of a synthesized powder deviates from 1.67, β-TCP or CaO forms as a by-product on firing, so controlling the composition is important.

biomaterials-004.question: Which statement correctly describes osseointegration, as the term is used for pure titanium in dental implants and similar devices?
choices: A state in which bone and the implant surface are in direct contact without intervening fibrous tissue and can transfer load
A state in which the implant gradually dissolves and is resorbed in the body and is replaced by new bone formed by osteoblasts
A state in which the gap between the implant and bone is filled with PMMA bone cement, fixing them by mechanical interlocking
biomaterials-004.explanation: Osseointegration is a phenomenon discovered by Brånemark with titanium, and it refers to a state in which living bone and the implant surface are in direct contact without intervening fibrous connective tissue and can transfer load. The titanium surface is covered by a TiO₂ passive film a few nm thick that is stable in body fluids, so bone forms along that surface. Moderately roughening the surface helps bone interlock with it and speeds fixation. The term mainly expresses direct contact with bone, as distinct from chemical bonding such as that of hydroxyapatite. Being resorbed in the body and replaced by bone is a property of bioresorbable materials such as β-TCP, and fixation with bone cement is a different method called cemented fixation.

biomaterials-005.question: When a metal with a Young's modulus far higher than that of bone is used for the stem of an artificial hip joint, which statement correctly describes the resulting problem of stress shielding?
choices: Bone carries most of the load, so excessive stress acts on the bone and it fractures easily
The implant carries most of the load and the stress on the surrounding bone falls, so the bone is resorbed and thins
The passive film on the implant surface breaks under stress, and the release of metal ions increases
biomaterials-005.explanation: When bone and an implant carry a load together, both strain by nearly the same amount, so the one with the larger Young's modulus carries most of the stress. The Young's modulus of cortical bone is about 10–30 GPa, but Co-Cr alloys at about 210 GPa and Ti-6Al-4V at about 110 GPa are far higher, so the stress on the bone becomes smaller than it should be. Bone changes the balance of formation and resorption according to the mechanical stimulus it receives (Wolff's law), so where the stimulus falls, bone is resorbed and thins, which causes implant loosening and fractures around the implant. Excessive stress on the bone is the opposite situation. Metal ion release due to damage to the passive film is a separate problem, such as fretting corrosion.

biomaterials-006.question: A rod of cortical bone (Young's modulus 20 GPa) and a rod of Ti-6Al-4V (Young's modulus 110 GPa) with the same cross-sectional area are joined in parallel and together carry a tensile load along their length. If both have the same strain, which value is closest to the fraction of the total load carried by the bone?
choices: About 85%
About 18%
About 15%
biomaterials-006.explanation: Because the strain ε is the same, each stress is proportional to the Young's modulus (σ = Eε), and since the cross-sectional areas are also equal, the loads are in the ratio 20 : 110. The bone's share is 20/(20 + 110) ≈ 0.154, about 15%. The implant takes over about 85% of the load that the bone alone used to carry, so the stimulus to the bone falls sharply and stress shielding occurs. About 85% is the share carried by the implant, and about 18% takes the modulus ratio 20/110 directly as the share. Switching to a β titanium alloy with a Young's modulus of about 55 GPa raises the bone's share to 20/75 ≈ 27%. The real shapes of bone and stem are complicated, but the idea that the difference in Young's modulus decides the load sharing is the same.

biomaterials-007.question: What is the main reason why β titanium alloys such as the Ti-Nb-Ta-Zr system have been developed for implants that fix bone?
choices: Retaining the BCC β phase down to room temperature makes the Young's modulus lower than that of Ti-6Al-4V and reduces stress shielding
The β phase has an HCP structure with strong atomic bonding, which raises the Young's modulus above that of Ti-6Al-4V and prevents implant deformation
The β phase prevents a passive film from forming on the titanium surface, which makes chemical bonding to bone easier
biomaterials-007.explanation: Titanium takes the HCP α phase at low temperature and the BCC β phase at high temperature, and adding large amounts of β-stabilizing elements such as Nb, Ta and Mo retains the β phase even at room temperature. β alloys have a Young's modulus of about 55–80 GPa, lower than that of the α+β alloy Ti-6Al-4V (about 110 GPa) and closer to that of bone (about 10–30 GPa), so they reduce stress shielding. Nb, Ta and Zr are also considered to have low cytotoxicity, with the added advantage of avoiding V and Al. It is the α phase that is HCP; calling the β phase HCP confuses the crystal structures. Raising the stiffness of an implant works in the direction of strengthening stress shielding. β alloys also form a passive film on their surface and keep their corrosion resistance, and losing the film would only increase ion release, not lead to bonding with bone.

biomaterials-008.question: Estimate the Young's modulus of porous titanium with open pores using the Gibson–Ashby equation E* = Es(ρ*/ρs)². If the Young's modulus of dense titanium is Es = 110 GPa and the porosity is 60%, which value is closest to E*? ρ*/ρs is the relative density.
choices: About 44 GPa
About 18 GPa
About 40 GPa
biomaterials-008.explanation: With a porosity of 60%, the relative density is ρ*/ρs = 1 − 0.60 = 0.40. E* = 110 × 0.40² = 110 × 0.16 ≈ 17.6 GPa, about 18 GPa, which falls within the range of the Young's modulus of cortical bone (about 10–30 GPa). Open pores also serve as a scaffold for bone to grow into, so porous metals are one way to reduce stress shielding. About 44 GPa forgets the square and uses 110 × 0.40, and about 40 GPa uses the porosity itself as 110 × 0.60². However, more porosity also lowers the strength, especially the fatigue strength, so the design is a balance between porosity and strength.

biomaterials-009.question: Which correctly describes the mechanism of superelasticity in the Ni-Ti alloy (about 50 at%Ni) used for orthodontic wires and stents? The service temperature is above the reverse transformation finish temperature Af.
choices: Plastic deformation by dislocation slip occurs, but in Ni-Ti the dislocations move back on unloading and the shape recovers
Fine precipitates stop dislocation motion, so the Young's modulus becomes larger than that of steel and the alloy deforms less
Under load the parent phase transforms to martensite (stress-induced martensitic transformation), and on unloading it reverts and the strain recovers
biomaterials-009.explanation: Above Af, the parent phase with the B2 structure is stable. When stress is applied, the parent phase transforms to martensite at a certain stress (stress-induced martensitic transformation), and a large strain develops at a nearly constant stress. On unloading the martensite becomes unstable and returns to the parent phase, so strains of up to about 6–8% recover. This property of deforming greatly and returning at a nearly constant force is used in orthodontic wires that move teeth with a constant force and in stents that are folded thin and inserted into blood vessels. Plastic deformation by dislocation slip is a permanent strain that does not recover on unloading. Strengthening with precipitates only raises the yield stress; the Young's modulus hardly changes, and it does not explain superelasticity.

biomaterials-010.question: Which statement correctly describes the low-temperature degradation that became a problem for yttria partially stabilized zirconia (Y-TZP) femoral heads in artificial hip joints?
choices: In a moist environment, tetragonal grains transform to monoclinic from the surface with a volume expansion, roughening the surface and lowering the strength
At about body temperature the tetragonal phase gradually changes to cubic, so transformation toughening at crack tips acts more strongly and the toughness rises
Chloride ions in body fluids cause pitting, and deep pits form on the surface
biomaterials-010.explanation: Y-TZP gets its high toughness from transformation toughening, in which metastable tetragonal grains transform to monoclinic and expand under the stress at a crack tip. In a moist environment, however, the tetragonal → monoclinic transformation proceeds slowly from the surface even at temperatures as low as body temperature. The volume expansion of about 4% creates microcracks and grain pull-out at the surface, roughening it and lowering the strength and wear resistance. This is low-temperature degradation (hydrothermal degradation); manufacturing conditions accelerated the transformation and fractures of femoral heads became a problem. For this reason, alumina–zirconia composites and similar materials have been developed. Transformation to the cubic phase does not occur at low temperature and does not strengthen transformation toughening. Pitting is corrosion in which the passive film of a metal breaks down locally; it is not a degradation mechanism of oxide ceramics.

biomaterials-011.question: Which statement about PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) bone cement used to fix artificial joints is correct?
choices: It bonds chemically to the surfaces of both bone and implant and fixes the two together as an adhesive, like an epoxy resin
PMMA melted by heating to about 200℃ is injected and fixes the implant as it cools to body temperature and solidifies into a glass
When PMMA powder is mixed with the liquid monomer, it polymerizes at room temperature and hardens while releasing heat
biomaterials-011.explanation: Bone cement is used by kneading PMMA powder with liquid methyl methacrylate (the monomer) during surgery. Addition polymerization by radicals generated from the initiator proceeds at room temperature, and the cement hardens in around 10 minutes. This polymerization is exothermic, and the points to watch are thermal damage to surrounding tissue from the temperature rise during hardening, residual monomer, and polymerization shrinkage. Bone cement does not bond chemically; as a filler that fills the space between the irregular bone surface and the implant and interlocks mechanically, it distributes and transfers the load to the bone. PMMA is a thermoplastic, but its melting temperature is far too high for use inside the body, so it is introduced as monomer and polymerized in the body.

biomaterials-012.question: What is the main reaction by which polylactic acid (PLA), used in absorbable sutures and bone fixation pins, degrades in the body?
choices: UV photodegradation of the main chain
Hydrolysis of the ester bonds in the main chain
Thermal decomposition (depolymerization) of the main chain at body temperature
biomaterials-012.explanation: In aliphatic polyesters such as PLA and polyglycolic acid (PGA), the ester bonds of the main chain are hydrolyzed by water in the body, the molecular weight falls, and they finally become lactic acid or glycolic acid. These are metabolized and ultimately leave the body as carbon dioxide and water. Hydrolysis proceeds even without enzymes, and because the acid of the carboxyl groups produced accelerates further degradation (autocatalysis), large parts can degrade from the inside. Ultraviolet light hardly reaches the inside of the body, so photodegradation is not a mechanism of degradation there. At 37℃ thermal decomposition (depolymerization) hardly occurs; it is a phenomenon to watch during molding at around 200℃.

biomaterials-013.question: A bone fixation pin of crystalline poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), made only of the L-isomer, takes several years to be fully resorbed in the body. Which is a correct way to make it degrade faster?
choices: Copolymerize with the D-isomer to make amorphous poly-DL-lactic acid
Raise the crystallinity by drawing or heat treatment, increasing the crystalline regions that are hydrolyzed
Increase the molecular weight to raise the number of ester bonds that hydrolysis can cleave
biomaterials-013.explanation: Hydrolysis proceeds first in the amorphous regions, which water penetrates easily, and is slow in the crystalline regions, where the chains are tightly packed. Poly-DL-lactic acid (PDLLA), copolymerized with the D-isomer, loses its stereoregularity and becomes amorphous, so it degrades faster. PLGA, copolymerized with glycolic acid, which has no methyl group and is more hydrophilic, also degrades faster. The degradation period of PLGA can be tuned from weeks to months by its composition, and it is also used as a carrier that releases drugs gradually. Raising the crystallinity makes it harder for water to enter, slowing degradation. Increasing the molecular weight raises the number of bonds that must be cut before strength is lost, so the loss of strength and the resorption are again slower.

biomaterials-014.question: Suppose the number-average molecular weight Mn of a biodegradable polymer falls by hydrolysis as Mn(t) = Mn₀exp(−kt). For k = 0.030 day⁻¹, which value is closest to the number of days until Mn falls to 20% of its initial value?
choices: About 23 days
About 27 days
About 54 days
biomaterials-014.explanation: From exp(−kt) = 0.20, t = ln(1/0.20)/k = ln 5/0.030 = 1.609/0.030 ≈ 53.6 days, about 54 days. About 23 days uses the common logarithm log 5 ≈ 0.699 instead of the natural logarithm. About 27 days assumes the molecular weight falls linearly in proportion to time, giving 0.80/0.030. In reality, acid accumulating inside a large part speeds up degradation there and crystallization proceeds during degradation, so the fall deviates from a simple exponential. Also, strength is lost later than the molecular weight falls, and mass loss (resorption) begins even later. For this reason the composition and molecular weight of the material are chosen so that it keeps its strength until the bone heals and is resorbed afterward.

biomaterials-015.question: Magnesium, studied as a biodegradable metal, corrodes in body fluids as Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂. When a 0.10 g magnesium screw corrodes completely, which value is closest to the volume of hydrogen released? Take the molar mass of Mg as 24.31 g/mol and the molar volume of gas at 37℃ and 1 atm as 25.4 L/mol.
choices: About 52 mL
About 104 mL
About 209 mL
biomaterials-015.explanation: The amount of Mg is 0.10/24.31 ≈ 4.11×10⁻³ mol. Mg gives up 2 electrons when it becomes Mg²⁺, and those electrons turn 2 H⁺ into 1 H₂ molecule, so 1 mol of H₂ is released per mol of Mg. The volume is 4.11×10⁻³ × 25.4 L ≈ 0.104 L, about 104 mL. Even a single screw releases this much gas, so fast corrosion causes the problem of gas accumulating in tissue, and research is under way to slow the corrosion to match bone healing by alloying and surface treatment. About 52 mL assumes 1 mol of H₂ forms from 2 mol of Mg, and about 209 mL is misled by the coefficient of 2H₂O into assuming 2 mol of H₂ per 1 mol of Mg.
